lines.note: Uerno completes go-uerno from f469, the government of the realm, Tenca. A new example, ya wo tamotsu, concerns holding an arrow; Tenca is a Japanese term embedded in Portuguese exposition.

runs.text: ou eſperar com a frecha no arco pera tirar.

lines.note: The arrow is kept on the bow while waiting to shoot. This completes the physical holding sense of tamotsu rather than the preceding government sense.
Go-okite wo tamotsu means observing the sacred law. The honorific Japanese formulation remains roman, while the Portuguese translation continues below.
Sancta completes the sacred-law gloss; inochi wo tamotsu then introduces preserving one's life. The close-set Inochiuotamotçu is retained as printed.
The life example is translated as living or remaining alive. The short continuation closes the series of tamotsu examples.
Tamochitodoke means persevering in keeping or observing something. The worn Portuguese verb is Perſeuerar, not the OCR's interrupted Perſeu rar.

runs.text: guarda, ou obſeruancia de algũa couſa.

lines.note: The perseverance concerns guarding or observing something. Obſeruancia has an i rather than the OCR's t in obſeruancta; the historical u/v spelling is preserved.

runs.text: Outros que não ſão parentes, nem da

lines.note: Tamon denotes outsiders who are not relatives. The t in Outros is visible despite weak impression and corrects OCR Ouros.

runs.text: meſma gèração. ¶ Item, Outra ſeita, ou

lines.note: The outsiders are not of the same lineage; a further sense concerns another sect. The scan supports ſeita, not OCR ſeuta, while the printed accent in gèração is retained.

runs.text: os de outra ſeita, ou inſtituto.

lines.note: The further sense includes people of another sect or institution. The word inſtituto contains the t omitted by OCR.

Tamoori is a variant for which the dictionary prefers tamawaru. The italic Meliùs states that preference, and Dar starts the explanation about giving by an honored person. Fine traces above the past-form o support retaining ǒtta, but that caron is substantially worn.
An honored person gives; the following qualification contrasts the register of tamawaru. Honrada and its following stop replace OCR honcada; the embedded Japanese verb remains roman.
Ve completes ſerue: tamawaru is more suited to writing and formal speech. Pera, not OCR peta, introduces those settings.
Tamot is something belonging to another, explained as ta no mono. The checked final t is retained rather than expanded into an extra syllable.
Tamoto is the pouch or hanging part of a sleeve. The Portuguese noun reads Bolſo, not OCR Balſo; the example begins tamoto wo.
Tamoto wo nurasu, wetting the sleeves, is glossed poetically as crying. The next expression begins 'the sleeves drying' and continues below; the local italic P. precedes its explanatory gloss.
Hima mo nashi completes the image of sleeves never having time to dry, meaning much weeping. A separate sleeve-grasping example begins after the paragraph mark.
Tamoto ni toritsuku or sugaru means clinging to someone's sleeves. The alternative marker l is not part of the Japanese verbs.
The Portuguese confirms grasping the sleeves, with das rather than OCR dos. Tamoto wo fi- begins another example of stopping someone by the sleeve.
Cayuru completes ficayuru, alternatively fiqitodomuru, holding someone back. The source's historical verb forms are not replaced by their modern equivalents.
The person is detained by pulling on the sleeves. This completes the last tamoto example before the offering entry.

runs.text: O que ſe offrece ao idolo, offerta,

lines.note: Tamuke is an offering presented to an idol, in the historical dictionary's terminology. The printed offrece is retained without supplying an unprinted internal vowel.
Ou ſacrificio adds sacrifice as another rendering of the offering. The short row belongs to the noun, not the following verb.
Tamuke gives the verb for offering or placing something before an object of worship. The headword has u, not the OCR's Tamaqe.
The offering is placed before an idol or a deceased person. Defuncto, not the OCR's deſtancto, is supported by the visible f and context; the example lists tea offerings and flowers.
Koo wo tamukuru completes the example of offering incense along with the preceding items. The verb's a corrects OCR i; Foto- begins a Japanese religious term embedded in the Portuguese gloss.

runs.text: que, ou do morto cha, & fulhas, ou pòs de hũa

lines.note: Que completes Fotoque, followed by offerings before the deceased: tea, foliage or flowers, and powdered wood. The worn plant word is read provisionally as fulhas, not OCR filhas; the ampersand after cha is visibly present.

runs.text: aruore como loureiro que poem ſobre a cinza,

lines.note: The incense material is compared with a laurel-like tree and is put on ash. This is the dictionary's descriptive comparison, not a modern botanical determination.

runs.text: & vai ardendo pouco a pouco. ¶ Item, Offe-

lines.note: The incense burns gradually. Ardendo restores the missing d in OCR arendo; a further sense of offering begins with Offe- at the right edge.
Recer completes offerecer, followed by making a sacrifice to God. The close-set fazerſacrificio is retained as printed.
Tamura means another settlement, explained by bechi no mura. The r in mura is worn but supported by its remaining stroke and the settlement gloss, correcting OCR muta.
Pouoação completes the alternative rendering as a settlement or village. The historical u/v spelling is retained.
Tamushi is a skin eruption, glossed empingem. The example tamushi ga dekuru describes its appearance; no modern diagnostic claim is imposed on the historical description.
The Portuguese first describes the eruption appearing, then tamushi ga hirogaru introduces its spreading. The nasal abbreviation marks and divided Estẽ- are retained.

runs.text: derſe, ou ir lastrando a empingẽ. ¶

lines.note: Derſe completes the spreading gloss. The worn middle of lastrando is restored from surviving traces and the sense of spreading, rather than retaining the OCR's la trando; a new example follows.

runs.text: Ir a empingẽ comẽdo, ou laurãdo.

lines.note: Tamushi ga kuimawaru describes the eruption spreading as though eating its way around. The Portuguese comẽdo and laurãdo preserve the same progressive image and their nasal abbreviations.

runs.text: Tinta vermelha clara em pò, que ſerue

lines.note: Tan is a light-red powdered pigment. The source identifies its material form but does not establish a modern chemical composition.
The pigment is also said to serve as medicine. This records the historical dictionary's use statement, not present-day treatment advice.
The homograph tan means phlegm; tan ga zzuru describes its coming out. A visible gap separates Tanga and zzuru, and the Portuguese begins the matching action.
Phlegm comes out through the mouth, completing the example. The old Portuguese spelling freimas is retained rather than modernized.
Tana is a cupboard or shelving structure. The source's Almario and parteleiro are preserved as historical spellings rather than corrected to modern Portuguese forms.

runs.text: Duas estrellas aßi chamadas que e-

lines.note: Tanabata is first defined through two named stars. Duas, not OCR Deus, gives the number; e- begins the verb continued on the next line.

runs.text: ſtão na via lactea de fronte hũa da outra.

lines.note: The two stars are described as facing one another on the Milky Way. The scan supports ſtão and lactea, correcting ſtio and ladea while retaining the source's phrasing.

runs.text: ¶ Item, O ſeptimo dia da ſeptima lua em que

lines.note: Tanabata also denotes the seventh day of the seventh lunar month. The worn phrase is ſeptima lua, not OCR ſeptimala, and ſeptimo has t rather than u.

runs.text: ſe aſoalha, ou tira fora fato, & roupa, &c.

lines.note: On that day, household goods and clothes are aired or brought outside. The historical aſoalha is retained rather than modernized.
Offerings are made to those stars. Tana- then begins the expression naming the festival day, continued below.

runs.text: Dia em que fazem esta ceremo-

lines.note: Batano fi completes Tanabata no hi, the day when the ceremony is performed. Fazem corrects OCR ſezem, and the small visible terminal hyphen preserves the division of ceremonia into column 2.
Nia completes ceremonia across the column boundary. Tanabata no matsuri introduces the name of the festival, with a second Ceremo- divided at this line end.

runs.text: nia, ou ſacrificio, & festa que fazem a eſtas

lines.note: The festival is glossed as a ceremony or sacrifice and celebration performed for the stars. The old Portuguese spelling and the printed festa type are preserved.
Estrellas completes the reference to the two stars of the preceding Tanabata entry. This short physical continuation is not a separate headword.
Tanabiki means to extend or trail through the air. The inflectional forms and the historical Eſtenderenſe are retained, with co- continuing into como below.

The examples are clouds, smoke, and a weather term provisionally retained as the printed-looking neuca. That unusual word is not silently modernized to nevoa; Fataga begins the flag example continued next.
Tanabiqu, with an initial t rather than OCR r, completes hata ga tanabiku. The Portuguese describes banners waving with the wind.
Vento completes the preceding explanation of flags fluttering in the wind. The isolated word and its full stop remain on their own physical row.
Tanagayeri denotes deterioration or degeneration of a stock or seed. The headword has e before ri, not OCR o, and leads into a broader Portuguese explanation below.

runs.text: degenerar algũa couſa como animal, fruita, &c.

lines.note: The definition extends to the degeneration of animals, fruit, and similar things. Degenerar is one word; fruita restores r from OCR i, and the small c after the ampersand is visible.
Inu ga tanagayeru is illustrated by a dog losing its ability to smell. The example is roman; the Portuguese explanation starts on this row and continues below.

runs.text: cheirar, ou de lhe dar o faro na cuça.

lines.note: The dog ceases to pick up a hunting scent. The vowel in the final word looks u in this copy, so cuça is retained as an anomalous or damaged reading rather than silently replaced with caça.
Tanago is the name of a fish. The scan shows a joined double-s form in aßi, correcting OCR aſi; no species identification is added to the diplomatic text.
Tanagocoro denotes the palms of the hands. The headword has c, not OCR t, and the following example begins Ta-, not Ti-, before the physical line break.
Nagocorouo completes the preceding Ta-; the whole phrase means bringing the palms together. The Portuguese also allows raising the hands, with aleuen- divided at the right edge.
Tar completes aleuentar, and tanagocoro ni nigiru introduces holding something in the palm. The entry moves from the literal gesture to possession in the following gloss.

runs.text: Estar de poße dalgũa couſa, ou tela ja nas mãos.

lines.note: The second example is explained as possessing something or already having it in one's hands. The source's tela and ja are preserved without modern accents or hyphenation.

The poetic verb tanagumori describes the sky becoming overcast. The worn paradigm is read otta rather than OCR cara; P. is upright, and toldandoo preserves the source's close-set final article. Lexical aid: NINJAL, Entry Words Data of Nippojisho, Hideyuki Ohshima and Taichi Aida, v202510, CC BY 4.0; the supplied scan remains authoritative for transcription.

runs.text: tempo de maneira que pareçẽ hũas diuiſẽes co

lines.note: The cloudy sky is compared with an arrangement of separate masses. Pareçẽ is chosen for the poorly inked par çẽ, with the intervening e weak; the unusual graphic form diuiſẽes and unhyphenated final co are retained.

runs.text: mo de grãos, ou ſemente hũa ſobre outra.

lines.note: Mo completes como without supplying a hyphen to the preceding row. The clouds resemble grains or seed piled one over another; the weak e in ſemente is restored, with the printed nasal mark in hũa retained.

runs.text: O meter nagoa ſemente de arroz

lines.note: Tanavoroxi denotes placing rice seed in water. The source clearly has v after Tana, not OCR x; the definition continues with the bags and soaking process below.

runs.text: em ſacos pera amolecer, & começar abrotar

lines.note: The rice seed is put into bags to soften and begin sprouting. The historical spellings pera and abrotar are retained without imposing modern word separation.

runs.text: pera depois ſe ſemear na terra.

lines.note: The soaked seed is then sown in the ground, completing the process description. This is a continuation of Tanavoroxi, not an independent agricultural term.
Tanbat and tanmat are alternatives glossed as beginning and end. The source's l, separates alternatives and is not silently changed to a modern conjunction.

runs.text: Impoſição que ſe poem por cada var-

lines.note: Tanbet denotes a levy assessed on each paddy field. The small i in Impoſição is visible and corrects OCR Impoſção; var- continues into varzea below.
Zea completes varzea, identifying a levy charged to cultivators by paddy field. The continuation remains indented and retains the historical lauradores.

Tanbo is explained by ake and kure, morning and evening. The source's Menhãa spelling is retained: the visible nasal mark is above the first a, not the second, despite the alternative pattern found elsewhere in the book.
Tanbo kore wo omou means thinking about something morning and evening. The Portuguese interprets that as always having it in mind, with cui- continued below.
Do completes cuido; desire or love motivates the continuing thought. Amando restores a single word from the OCR's a mando, while the unusual iste is retained as printed.
Bo completes tanbo, and yukashii introduces longing. Denoite has n rather than OCR m, pairing day and night in the Portuguese gloss.
Saudades completes the description of persistent longing. The short continuation belongs to the preceding example and is not a new entry.
Tanka is explained as mijikai uta, short verse or song. Cantigas has a, not OCR u, and the adjective specifying brevity continues on the next row.
Breues completes the definition of short verses or songs. Its terminal point is preserved, and the next entry begins on a separate physical line.
Tancat is explained as short, patched clothing through mijikai tsuzure. The printed vocabulary and the opening Vestido curto are retained without modernizing the clothing term.
The garment is patched, completing the previous definition. Remendado has d rather than OCR l; the final S. is an upright register label, not part of the italic Portuguese gloss.
Tanchǒ and chǒtan are alternative orderings of the compound for short and long, explained by mijikai and nagai. The scan supports the retained vowel marks and the divided Cur-.
To completes curto, paired with comprido for short and long. This brief row finishes the entry without any omitted separate headword.
Tancu is a short saying or passage, explained by mijikai ku. Breue begins with B, not OCR P; the nasalized example fragment Tã- is wholly roman rather than partly italic.

The example says a short phrase contains extensive meaning. The damaged consonant in fucumu retains a curved trace consistent with c and the verb 'contain', correcting OCR furumu; Breue likewise corrects Freue.

runs.text: chea de muito miſterio, ou de muita materia.

lines.note: The short sentence is nevertheless full of meaning or substantial material. The source's miſterio is preserved as its explanatory wording rather than replaced by a modern translation of the Japanese.
Tandacu suru describes standing respectfully with the hands crossed. The headword has T, not OCR F, and cruzadas restores the worn but continuous word misread as craza las.
The posture is shown in someone's presence. The following example begins Fo-, chosen from the worn initial and the North-Star context; OCR ſin- would not form the ensuing Focuxinno.

runs.text: cuxinno ſono tocoroni ite xuxeino tanda-

lines.note: Together with Fo-, cuxinno identifies the North Star in an example about remaining in its place while the other stars pay respect. The letters near tanda- are weak, but the source's line division is retained.

Cu completes tandacu, and suru ga gotoshi expresses the comparison. The Portuguese begins its explanation with the North Star, confirming the referent without adding a source title to the transcription.

runs.text: eſtando quieta em ſeu lugar, todas as estrellas

lines.note: The North Star remains quiet in its place while all the stars attend it. The historical eſtando and the baseline estrella typography are preserved.

runs.text: ſe baquerã diante della, aßi deſta maneira, &c.

lines.note: The stars are described as bowing before it. Baquerã is the chosen reading of the weak middle letters, retaining the source's unusual verbal form; aßi deſta restores the visibly damaged comparison formula rather than OCR aſs d ſta.
Tandai is glossed by administrative offices, governor or corregedor. The latter word has e in its final middle syllable, correcting OCR corregador without changing the source's historical comparison.
Tandaye means investigating or inquiring. Peſquiſar has long s rather than OCR j, and the worn inquirir is read as the accompanying Portuguese synonym; the faint separator is taken as a comma.
